summary.text: The indices are split into multiples of \(p\) and unit residue blocks, where product expansions of the binomial factors, congruences for reciprocal power sums, and telescoping identities for weighted binomial moments show that all lower-order contributions cancel, leaving divisibility by \(p^{3r+3}\). The exceptional base cases \((p,r)=(3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) are settled by direct finite evaluation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
b(n,k)=\binom{n+k-1}{k},\qquad f(x)=3x^2+2x^3,
\]
so that
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}f(b(n,k)).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 3\) and every \(r\geq2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]

Throughout the proof, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers, extended by \(v_p(0)=+\infty\). We write
\[
x\equiv_e y
\]
when \(v_p(x-y)\geq e\). This notation is allowed for integral or even negative integral \(e\). We shall repeatedly use the elementary facts
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(x+y)&\geq\min(v_p(x),v_p(y)),\\
v_p(xy)&=v_p(x)+v_p(y),
\end{aligned}
\]
and the fact that the reciprocal of an integer not divisible by \(p\) has valuation zero. All rational expressions below have denominators prime to \(p\), apart from explicitly displayed powers of \(p\).

We first establish the auxiliary estimates needed for the main block decomposition.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Power sums and reciprocal sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put
\[
P_k(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^k.
\]
Reduction modulo \(p\), followed by the usual finite-field power-sum identity, gives
\[
P_k(p)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0<k<p-1).
\]
Indeed, multiplication by a generator of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) permutes the nonzero residues, and the resulting geometric-series argument shows that the sum of the \(k\)-th powers is zero unless \(p-1\mid k\).

Splitting \(0,\ldots,p^v m-1\) into blocks of length \(p\), and expanding \((pj+i)^k\), gives by induction
\[
v_p(P_k(p^v m))\geq v\quad (k<p-1),
\]
and, without the restriction on \(k\),
\[
v_p(P_k(p^v m))\geq v-1.
\]
We also need the elementary exact formulas
\[
2P_1(n)=n(n-1),
\]
\[
3(P_1(n)+P_2(n))=n^3-n,
\]
\[
4P_3(n)=n^2(n-1)^2.
\]
They follow either from the standard formulas for sums of powers or by induction after replacing \(n\) by \(n+1\). In particular, if \(p^v\mid n\) and \(p\geq3\), then
\[
v_p(P_1(n))\geq v,
\qquad
v_p(P_3(n))\geq2v.
\tag{1}
\]

For \(L,m\geq0\), define the reciprocal sum over the integers below \(L\) which are prime to \(p\) by
\[
H_m(L)=\sum_{\substack{0\leq i<L\\p\nmid i}}\frac1{i^m}.
\]
When \(m>0\), the zero term is harmlessly interpreted as zero; equivalently the sum runs over \(1\leq i<L\), \(p\nmid i\). In particular,
\[
H_m(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac1{i^m}.
\]
Because inversion permutes \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), the same finite-field power-sum argument gives
\[
v_p(H_m(p))\geq1\qquad(0<m<p-1).
\tag{2}
\]
The same conclusion holds for every odd \(m\) when \(p\geq3\), since pairing \(i\) with \(-i\) modulo \(p\) makes the sum equal to its negative and 2 is invertible.

To estimate longer reciprocal sums, split them into blocks:
\[
H_m(pl)=\sum_{a=0}^{l-1}\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}(pa+j)^{-m}.
\]
For any positive integer \(K\), the binomial expansion of the reciprocal gives
\[
(pa+j)^{-m}
\equiv_K
\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(-1)^k\binom{m+k-1}{k}(pa)^k j^{-m-k}.
\]
Summing first over \(a\) and then over \(j\) yields
\[
H_m(pl)\equiv_K
\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}(-1)^k\binom{m+k-1}{k}p^kP_k(l)H_{m+k}(p).
\tag{3}
\]
The discarded terms all contain at least \(p^K\), while their denominators are \(p\)-adic units.

A second useful expansion comes from reflection. If \(p\mid L\), then \(i\mapsto L-i\) permutes the indices occurring in \(H_m(L)\). Thus
\[
H_m(L)=\sum_{\substack{0<i<L\\p\nmid i}}(L-i)^{-m}.
\]
If \(v_p(L)\geq q\geq1\), expansion in powers of \(L/i\) gives
\[
H_m(L)\equiv_{qK}
(-1)^m\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\binom{m+k-1}{k}L^kH_{m+k}(L).
\tag{4}
\]
From (2)--(4) one obtains the following bounds. If \(p^{v+1}\mid L\), then
\[
v_p(H_m(L))\geq v
\tag{5}
\]
for every \(m\), and
\[
v_p(H_m(L))\geq2v+1
\tag{6}
\]
for odd \(m\). If \(p\geq5\), then additionally
\[
v_p(H_2(L))\geq v+1,
\qquad
v_p(H_1(L))\geq2v+2.
\tag{7}
\]
For \(p=3\), the corresponding uniform statements lose one power of \(p\). It is convenient to put
\[
\epsilon=\begin{cases}1,&p=3,\\0,&p\ne3.\end{cases}
\]
Then, for all \(p\geq3\),
\[
v_p(H_2(L))\geq v+1-\epsilon,
\qquad
v_p(H_1(L))\geq2v+2-\epsilon.
\tag{8}
\]

For completeness, (5) follows directly from (3): the \(k=0\) term is \(lH_m(p)\), and every later term contains enough powers from \(p^kP_k(l)\). If both \(H_m(p)\) and \(H_{m+1}(p)\) vanish modulo \(p\), the same calculation gains one power, giving the first part of (7). Formula (4) with odd \(m\), after moving its constant term to the left, gives
\[
2H_m(L)\equiv LmH_{m+1}(L)
\]
to the required precision; (5) applied to \(H_{m+1}\) gives (6), and the case \(m=1\) together with the stronger estimate for \(H_2\) gives the second part of (7). Since 2 is a unit, it may be cancelled.

Two more precise reflection consequences, obtained by retaining respectively four and six terms in (4), are
\[
H_3(L)\equiv_{4v+3}-\frac{3L}{2}H_4(L),
\tag{9}
\]
\[
H_1(L)\equiv_{6v+5}-\frac L2H_2(L)+\frac{L^3}{4}H_4(L),
\tag{10}
\]
whenever \(p^{v+1}\mid L\). The omitted terms are controlled by (5) and (6), and 2 and 4 are units because \(p\geq3\).

Define
\[
\alpha=\frac{H_2(p)}p-pH_4(p),
\qquad
\beta=\frac{H_4(p)}p.
\tag{11}
\]
Using (3), (1), (9), and (10), one obtains, whenever \(p^v\mid l\),
\[
H_4(pl)\equiv_{v+2-\epsilon}\beta\,pl,
\tag{12}
\]
\[
H_2(pl)\equiv_{v+4-\epsilon}\alpha\,pl+\beta(pl)^3,
\tag{13}
\]
and
\[
H_1(pl)\equiv_{2v+5-\epsilon}
-\frac\alpha2(pl)^2-\frac\beta4(pl)^4.
\tag{14}
\]
Let us indicate the cancellation in (13), the least immediate of these formulas. Keeping four terms in (3) gives
\[
H_2(pl)\equiv
lH_2(p)-2pP_1(l)H_3(p)+3p^2P_2(l)H_4(p)-4p^3P_3(l)H_5(p).
\]
The last term has the required valuation. Formula (9), with \(L=p\), replaces \(H_3(p)\) by \(-3pH_4(p)/2\). The identity
\(3(P_1(l)+P_2(l))=l^3-l\) then turns the remaining expression into
\[
lH_2(p)+p^2(l^3-l)H_4(p)=\alpha pl+\beta(pl)^3.
\]
Formula (12) is the first term of (3); formula (14) follows by substituting (12) and (13) into (10).

We shall use
\[
v_p(\alpha)\geq-\epsilon,
\qquad
v_p(\beta)\geq-1.
\tag{15}
\]
For \(p\geq7\), (2) with \(m=4\) improves the second bound to
\[
v_p(\beta)\geq0.
\tag{16}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Finite harmonic sums and one special congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write
\[
h_m(n)=\sum_{i=1}^n i^{-m},
\]
and define the ordered multiple harmonic sums
\[
h_{a,b}(n)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}i^{-a}j^{-b},
\]
\[
h_{a,b,c}(n)=\sum_{1\leq i<j<k\leq n}i^{-a}j^{-b}k^{-c}.
\]
Thus \(H_m(p)=h_m(p-1)\). Multiplication of sums gives the shuffle identity
\[
h_{a,b}(n)+h_{b,a}(n)+h_{a+b}(n)=h_a(n)h_b(n).
\tag{17}
\]
Reflection \((i,j)\mapsto(p-j,p-i)\) gives
\[
h_{a,b}(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{a+b}h_{b,a}(p-1)\pmod p.
\tag{18}
\]
Combining (2), (17), and (18), for \(p\geq7\) one obtains
\[
h_{2,2}(p-1)\equiv0,
\qquad
h_{1,3}(p-1)\equiv h_{3,1}(p-1)\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{19}
\]
A standard alternating-binomial identity also gives
\[
h_{1,1,2}(p-1)\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{20}
\]
Here is a derivation. Define
\[
\mathcal B_n(g)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\binom n{k+1}g(k+1).
\]
Pascal's identity and summation by parts imply
\[
\mathcal B_n(k^{-1})=h_1(n),
\]
\[
\mathcal B_n(k^{-2})=
\sum_{j=1}^n j^{-1}h_1(j),
\]
and a second application gives the corresponding depth-three identity
\[
\mathcal B_n(k^{-1}h_3(k))
=
 h_{1,1,2}(n)+h_{2,2}(n)+h_{1,3}(n)+h_4(n).
\]
For \(n=p-1\),
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k+1}\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
so the left side is congruent to the negative of its ordinary prefix sum. Reversing that prefix sum produces \(h_{3,1}(p-1)+h_4(p-1)\). Now (19) and \(h_4(p-1)\equiv0\) imply (20).

We require the sharper relation
\[
v_p\bigl(2h_{1,2}(p-1)-3\alpha\bigr)\geq1
\qquad(p\geq5),
\tag{21}
\]
and
\[
v_p\bigl(2h_{1,2}(p-1)-3\alpha\bigr)\geq2
\qquad(p\geq7).
\tag{22}
\]
To prove it, expand
\[
F(x,n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1+\frac xi\right)
\]
to second order:
\[
F(x,n)\equiv_{3v_p(x)}1+xh_1(n)+x^2h_{1,1}(n).
\tag{23}
\]
Insert (23), with \(x=-p\), into the alternating binomial transform of \(k^{-2}\). The identities above and (17) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
&2p h_{1,2}(p-1)-3h_2(p-1)+2p h_3(p-1)\\
&\quad-2p^2\bigl(h_{1,1,2}(p-1)+h_{1,3}(p-1)\bigr)-h_1(p-1)^2
\equiv0\pmod {p^3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]
On replacing \(3\alpha\) by
\(3H_2(p)/p-3pH_4(p)\), multiplying the desired relation by \(p\), and using (24), the difference consists of terms involving \(h_1^2\), \(ph_3\), \(p^2h_{1,1,2}\), \(p^2h_{1,3}\), and \(p^2h_4\). For \(p\geq5\), (2), (6), and the integrality of the multiple sums make these divisible by \(p^2\), proving (21). For \(p\geq7\), use the stronger facts
\[
v_p(h_1(p-1))\geq2,
\quad v_p(h_3(p-1))\geq2,
\]
together with (19), (20), and \(v_p(h_4(p-1))\geq1\); the terms are then divisible by \(p^3\), proving (22).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Binomial products and low moments
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The product \(F\) satisfies
\[
F(n,k)=\binom{n+k}{k},
\qquad
b(n,k+1)=\frac n{k+1}F(n,k),
\tag{25}
\]
\[
F(n,k+1)-F(n,k)=b(n,k+1),
\tag{26}
\]
and
\[
(k+1)F(n,k+1)=(n+k+1)F(n,k).
\tag{27}
\]
If \(0<k<p^s\), then \(v_p(k)<s\), and hence
\[
v_p\bigl(b(p^s,k)\bigr)\geq s-v_p(k)\geq1,
\qquad
F(p^s,k)\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{28}
\]

Define
\[
X_m(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(n/k)^m,
\]
again taking the \(k=0\) term to be zero for \(m>0\). Splitting indices according as \(p\mid k\) gives the exact recursion
\[
X_m(pt)=X_m(t)+(pt)^mH_m(pt).
\tag{29}
\]
Using (5)--(8) inductively in (29),
\[
v_p(X_m(p^s))\geq m,
\tag{30}
\]
\[
v_p(X_2(p^s))\geq3\quad(p\geq5),
\qquad
v_p(X_3(p^s))\geq4\quad(p\geq3).
\tag{31}
\]
Since \(p^s\) is odd,
\[
b(p^s,p^s)=
\prod_{i=1}^{p^s-1}\left(1-(p^s/i)^2\right).
\]
Expanding this product through its linear term and using (30) gives
\[
b(p^s,p^s)\equiv_4 1-X_2(p^s).
\tag{32}
\]
Consequently \(b(p^s,p^s)\equiv1\pmod {p^2}\), and modulo \(p^3\) when \(p\geq5\).

Put
\[
S_m(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n b(n,k)^m,
\qquad
A(n)=3S_2(n)+2S_3(n)=a(n).
\]
From (25), (28), and a first-order product expansion,
\[
S_m(p^s)\equiv_{m+1}1+b(p^s,p^s)^m+X_m(p^s).
\tag{33}
\]
Equations (31)--(33) imply
\[
A(p^s)\equiv_{3+\epsilon}10,
\tag{34}
\]
and, since \(F(p^s,p^s)=2b(p^s,p^s)\),
\[
f(F(p^s,p^s))\equiv_{3+\epsilon}28.
\tag{35}
\]
Thus
\[
A(p^s)-f(F(p^s,p^s))\equiv_{3+\epsilon}-18.
\tag{36}
\]
For \(p\geq5\), (34)--(35) follow immediately from the mod-\(p^3\) version of (32), (31), and (33). For \(p=3\), the coefficient 3 in front of \(S_2\) supplies the missing factor, while (30)--(31) control the remaining terms; this gives precision \(p^4\), exactly as asserted.

Now define moments
\[
M_d(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k^dF(n,k)^2,
\qquad
U(n)=\frac{M_0(n)}n,

aqquad
V(n)=\frac{3M_2(n)+3M_1(n)+M_0(n)}n.
\]
(The stray letter in the displayed line is immaterial; the definition is \(V(n)=(3M_2+3M_1+M_0)/n\).)
Telescoping (26)--(27) gives the exact identities
\[
2(2n+1)M_0(n)=n\bigl(F(n,n)^2+S_2(n)\bigr),
\tag{37}
\]
\[
2(n+1)M_1(n)+(n+1)^2M_0(n)=n^2F(n,n)^2,
\tag{38}
\]
\[
(2n+3)M_2(n)+(n+1)(n+3)M_1(n)+(n+1)^2M_0(n)
=n^3F(n,n)^2.
\tag{39}
\]
For example, (38) follows by summing
\[
(k+1)^2F(n,k+1)^2-k^2F(n,k)^2
=\bigl(2(n+1)k+(n+1)^2\bigr)F(n,k)^2;
\]
the other two are obtained in the same way from linear and cubic telescoping expressions.

From (34), (37)--(39), noting that \(2n+1\) and \(n+1\) are units, one gets, for \(s\geq1\),
\[
(2p^s+1)U(p^s)\equiv_3 3,
\tag{40}
\]
\[
v_p(M_0(p^s))\geq s+\epsilon,
\qquad
v_p(M_1(p^s))\geq s+\epsilon,
\tag{41}
\]
\[
v_p(M_2(p^s))\geq s,
\qquad
v_p(V(p^s))\geq s,
\tag{42}
\]
provided either \(p\ne3\) or \(s\geq2\). If \(p=3\), the factor \(2p^s+3\) appearing when (39) is solved for \(M_2\) has valuation one; the extra assumption \(s\geq2\) and the \(\epsilon=1\) gain in (41) compensate exactly. This explains the sole exceptional low-exponent case in the general argument.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Products over indices prime to \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define
\[
Q(n,L)=\prod_{\substack{0<i<L\\p\nmid i}}\left(1+\frac ni\right).
\]
The elementary-symmetric expansion of a product says
\[
\prod_i(1+x_i)=1+e_1+e_2+e_3+\cdots,
\]
where
\[
2e_2=e_1^2-\sum_i x_i^2,
\]
\[
6e_3=e_1^3-3e_1\sum_i x_i^2+2\sum_i x_i^3,
\]
and
\[
24e_4=e_1^4-6e_1^2\sum_i x_i^2+3\left(\sum_i x_i^2\right)^2
+8e_1\sum_i x_i^3-6\sum_i x_i^4.
\]
Together with (5)--(8), these formulas give the second-order approximation, for \(r\geq2\), \(v<r\), and \(p^{v+1}\mid L\),
\[
Q(p^r,L)\equiv_{r+2v+5-\epsilon}
1+p^rH_1(L)-\frac{p^{2r}}2H_2(L).
\tag{43}
\]
Substitution of (13)--(14), when \(L=pl\) and \(p^v\mid l\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q(p^r,pl)\equiv_{r+2v+5-\epsilon}1
&-\frac\alpha2p^r(pl)(p^r+pl)\\
&-\frac\beta4p^r(pl)^3(pl+2p^r).
\end{aligned}
\tag{44}
\]
Also
\[
Q(p^r,L)\equiv_{r+2v+2-\epsilon}1.
\tag{45}
\]

Splitting a product into factors whose indices are divisible by \(p\) and factors whose indices are not gives the exact identity
\[
b(pn,pl)=b(n,l)Q(pn,pl).
\tag{46}
\]
Taylor expansion of \(f(xQ)-f(x)\), using (44)--(45), now gives the following termwise formula. If \(p^v\mid l\), \(v<r\), and \(v_p(x)\geq r-v-1\), then, modulo \(p^{3r+3}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(xQ(p^r,pl))-f(x)
\equiv{}&-3\alpha p^r(x^2+x^3)(pl)(p^r+pl)\\
&-\frac32\beta p^r(x^2+x^3)(pl)(p^r+pl)
\bigl((pl)^2+p^r(pl)+p^{2r}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{47}
\]
The identity is obtained by writing \(Q=1+z\). The linear part of
\(f(x(1+z))-f(x)\) is \(6(x^2+x^3)z\); all quadratic and cubic powers of \(z\) have valuation at least \(3r+3\) by (45). The difference between the displayed \(\beta\)-polynomial and the direct linear term from (44) is also of that valuation by (15).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Contribution of indices divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Set \(N=p^s\), \(P=p^{s+1}=pN\), where \(s\geq1\). For \(0\leq k<N\), apply (47) with
\[
r=s+1,
\quad l=k+1,
\quad v=v_p(k+1),
\quad x=b(N,k+1).
\]
The required bound on \(x\) is precisely (28), and (46) says
\[
b(P,p(k+1))=b(N,k+1)Q(P,p(k+1)).
\]
Using
\[
b(n,k+1)^2(k+1)(n+k+1)=n^2F(n,k)F(n,k+1),
\tag{48}
\]
which follows from (25) and (27), the \(\alpha\)-part of (47) becomes
\[
-3\alpha P^3F(N,k)F(N,k+1)(1+b(N,k+1)).
\]
Define
\[
W(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}F(n,k)F(n,k+1)(1+b(n,k+1)).
\]
An exact telescoping calculation using (26) gives
\[
W(n)=M_0(n)-\frac{A(n)-f(F(n,n))}{6}.
\tag{49}
\]
Indeed, term by term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(b(n,k+1))-&\bigl(f(F(n,k+1))-f(F(n,k))\bigr)\\
&=6\bigl(F(n,k)^2-F(n,k)F(n,k+1)(1+b(n,k+1))\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
and summing telescopes.

The \(\beta\)-part is a constant times
\[
W_B(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}F(n,k)F(n,k+1)(1+b(n,k+1))
\bigl((k+1)^2+n(k+1)+n^2\bigr).
\]
Another use of (25)--(27) shows
\[
v_p(W_B(N))\geq s.
\tag{50}
\]
More explicitly, each summand differs modulo \(p^s\) from
\((k+1)^2F(N,k+1)^2\); summing the latter gives
\(M_2(N)+N^2F(N,N)^2\), whose valuation is at least \(s\) by (42).
By (15)--(16), (50), and the assumption
\[
p\geq7\quad\hbox{or}\quad s\geq2,
\tag{51}
\]
the total \(\beta\)-part is divisible by \(p^{3s+6}\). Consequently (47)--(49) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{l=0}^{N}\bigl(f(b(P,pl))-f(b(N,l))\bigr)\\
&\qquad\equiv_{3s+6}
P^3\left\{\frac\alpha2\bigl(A(N)-f(F(N,N))\bigr)-3\alpha M_0(N)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{52}
\]
The \(l=0\) terms cancel, so the preceding termwise summation covers the whole left side.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Contribution of indices not divisible by \(p\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a block numbered \(l\), put
\[
B_m(l)=H_m(p(l+1))-H_m(pl)
=\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}(pl+j+1)^{-m}.
\tag{53}
\]
Also define
\[
B_{12}(l)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}(pl+j+1)^{-2}
\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}(pl+i+1)^{-1}.
\tag{54}
\]
For \(0\leq j<p-1\), product splitting gives
\[
b(P,pl+j+1)=\frac{P}{pl+j+1}F(N,l)Q(P,pl+j+1).
\tag{55}
\]
Expanding \(Q^2\) through quadratic order and \(Q^3\) through linear order yields
\[
Q(P,L)^2\equiv_{3(s+1)}1+2PH_1(L)+P^2(2H_1(L)^2-H_2(L)),
\tag{56}
\]
\[
Q(P,L)^3\equiv_{2(s+1)}1+3PH_1(L).
\tag{57}
\]
Substitution into \(f(b(P,pl+j+1))\), followed by summation over \(j\), gives, modulo \(p^{3s+6}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}f(b(P,pl+j+1))\equiv{}&
3P^2F(N,l)^2B_2(l)\\
&+6P^3F(N,l)^2H_1(pl)B_2(l)\\
&+6P^3F(N,l)^2B_{12}(l)\\
&+2P^3F(N,l)^3B_3(l).
\end{aligned}
\tag{58}
\]
The terms of fourth order in \(P\) are harmless. They are sums built from
\[
\sum_j(pl+j+1)^{-2}\bigl(2H_1(pl+j+1)^2-H_2(pl+j+1)\bigr)
\]
and
\[
\sum_j(pl+j+1)^{-3}H_1(pl+j+1).
\]
They are integral; if \(s\geq2\), the factor \(P^4\) alone reaches the required precision. If \(s=1\) and \(p\geq7\), reducing the inner sums modulo \(p\), using (19)--(20), shows that each is divisible by \(p\), again giving the required precision. This is exactly where condition (51) is used in the unit blocks.

We now sum (58) over \(0\leq l<N\). Four weighted block estimates are needed:
\[
\begin{aligned}
3P^2\sum_lF(N,l)^2B_2(l)
&\equiv_{3s+6}3\alpha P^2pM_0(N),
\tag{59}\\
\sum_lF(N,l)^2H_1(pl)B_2(l)&\equiv_{3-\epsilon}0,
\tag{60}\\
\sum_lF(N,l)^2B_{12}(l)
&\equiv_3 h_{1,2}(p-1)M_0(N),
\tag{61}\\
\sum_lF(N,l)^3B_3(l)&\equiv_3 0.
\tag{62}
\end{aligned}
\]
We justify these in turn.

From (13), let
\[
E(l)=H_2(pl)-\alpha pl-\beta(pl)^3.
\]
If \(p^v\mid l\), then \(v_p(E(l))\geq v+4-\epsilon\). Discrete summation by parts, together with
\[
v_p(F(N,l+1)^2-F(N,l)^2)\geq s-v_p(l+1),
\]
therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_lF(N,l)^2B_2(l)
\equiv_{s+4-\epsilon}{}&
\alpha pM_0(N)\\
&+\beta p^3\bigl(3M_2(N)+3M_1(N)+M_0(N)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{63}
\]
The second line is \(\beta p^3NV(N)\), and (15)--(16), (42), and (51) show that after multiplication by \(3P^2\) it vanishes modulo \(p^{3s+6}\). This proves (59).

For (60), if \(p\ne3\), equations (8) and (53) immediately give valuation at least 3 term by term. If \(p=3\), condition (51) gives \(s\geq2\). Substitute the leading term
\[
H_1(pl)\equiv_2-\frac\alpha2p^2l^2
\]
from (14), and \(B_2(l)\equiv H_2(p)\pmod p\); the weighted sum is then controlled by \(M_2(N)\), which has valuation at least \(s\). This proves (60).

For (61), expand each reciprocal in (54) to second order in \(pl\). One gets
\[
B_{12}(l)\equiv_3
h_{1,2}(p-1)-plD_4+(pl)^2D_5,
\tag{64}
\]
where
\[
D_4=h_{2,2}(p-1)+2h_{1,3}(p-1),
\]
\[
D_5=h_{3,2}(p-1)+2h_{2,3}(p-1)+3h_{1,4}(p-1).
\]
Both are integral, and \(D_4\equiv0\pmod p\) when \(p\geq7\), by (19). Multiplying (64) by \(F(N,l)^2\) and summing, the constant term is the right side of (61), while the other terms are \(-pD_4M_1(N)+p^2D_5M_2(N)\). Equations (41)--(42), with either side of (51), show that both have valuation at least 3. Thus (61) follows.

Finally, expanding (53) for \(m=3\), and using (9), gives
\[
B_3(l)\equiv_3-\frac{3p}{2}H_4(p)(2l+1).
\tag{65}
\]
The weighted sum of \((2l+1)F(N,l)^3\) has valuation at least \(\min(s,2)\). To see this, first telescope (27) to obtain the corresponding bound for the first power of \(F\), then use \(F(N,l)\equiv1\pmod p\) and the factorization
\[
F^3-3F+2=(F-1)^2(F+2).
\]
Combining this with (65), (2), and (51) proves (62).

Using (59)--(62) in (58), we obtain the total contribution of indices not divisible by \(p\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{l=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}f(b(P,pl+j+1))\\
&\qquad\equiv_{3s+6}
3\alpha P^2pM_0(N)+6P^3h_{1,2}(p-1)M_0(N).
\end{aligned}
\tag{66}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. The final cancellation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The interval \(0\leq k\leq P\) is the disjoint union of the multiples \(pl\), \(0\leq l\leq N\), and the unit indices \(pl+j+1\), \(0\leq l<N\), \(0\leq j<p-1\). Hence (52) and (66) show that
\[
A(P)-A(N)\equiv_{3s+6}P^3\Delta,
\]
where, because \(P^2p=P^3/N\),
\[
\Delta=
\frac\alpha2\bigl(A(N)-f(F(N,N))\bigr)
+3\alpha\left(\frac1N-1\right)M_0(N)
+6h_{1,2}(p-1)M_0(N).
\tag{67}
\]
We claim
\[
v_p(\Delta)\geq3.
\tag{68}
\]

By (36),
\[
\frac\alpha2\bigl(A(N)-f(F(N,N))+18\bigr)
\]
has valuation at least 3, using (15). By (40),
\[
3\alpha\bigl((2N+1)U(N)-3\bigr)
\]
also has valuation at least 3. Finally, (21)--(22), together with (41), imply
\[
\bigl(6h_{1,2}(p-1)-9\alpha\bigr)M_0(N)
\]
has valuation at least 3. Indeed, when \(p\geq7\), use (22) and \(v_p(M_0(N))\geq s\geq1\); when \(p=5\) and \(s\geq2\), use (21); when \(p=3\) and \(s\geq2\), both coefficients have valuation at least one and \(v_p(M_0(N))\geq s+1\).

Adding these three divisible quantities and using \(M_0(N)=NU(N)\), their sum simplifies exactly to \(\Delta\). Explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac\alpha2(A(N)-f(F(N,N))+18)
+3\alpha((2N+1)U(N)-3)\\
&\qquad +(6h_{1,2}-9\alpha)M_0(N)\\
&=\frac\alpha2(A(N)-f(F(N,N)))
+3\alpha\left(\frac1N-1\right)M_0(N)
+6h_{1,2}M_0(N).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (68) holds. Since \(v_p(P^3)=3(s+1)\), we conclude
\[
v_p(A(p^{s+1})-A(p^s))\geq3(s+1)+3=3s+6
\tag{69}
\]
whenever \(s\geq1\) and either \(p\geq7\) or \(s\geq2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Exceptional base cases and conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Take \(s=r-1\). If \(r\geq3\), then \(s\geq2\), so (69) applies to every prime \(p\geq3\). If \(r=2\) and \(p\geq7\), it also applies.

It remains only to check \((p,r)=(3,2)\) and \((5,2)\).

For \(p=3\), the binomial rows needed are
\[
(b(3,k))_{k=0}^3=(1,3,6,10),
\]
\[
(b(9,k))_{k=0}^9=(1,9,45,165,495,1287,3003,6435,12870,24310).
\]
Substitution into \(\sum_k(3b(n,k)^2+2b(n,k)^3)\) gives
\[
a(3)=2926,
\qquad
a(9)=33590792825200.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(9)-a(3)=33590792822274
=3^9\cdot1706589078.
\]

For \(p=5\), exact evaluation of the same finite sum (the binomial coefficients may be generated successively from \(b(n,0)=1\) by
\(b(n,k+1)=b(n,k)(n+k)/(k+1)\)) gives
\[
a(5)=4846260,
\]
\[
a(25)=581553752659150682384860284864053981408760.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(25)-a(5)
&=581553752659150682384860284864053976562500\\
&=5^9\cdot297755521361485149381048465850395636.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the desired congruence also holds in both exceptional cases.

Finally, \(A(n)=a(n)\) by definition, and (69), with \(s=r-1\), says precisely
\[
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})\equiv0\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
This proves the conjecture for every prime \(p\geq3\) and every integer \(r\geq2\).
